title: How long it takes
hook: the full Nitnem takes an hour or more, and traditions differ slightly on which banis are included

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime song. Your line was the night song. Did Sohila, or a minute of quiet, beat the scroll last night? Day one hundred thirty-six.

Let's do the math honestly, the way you'd look at a recipe before you start cooking. You've now met all the Nitnem banis: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. That's a lot of words, spread from before breakfast to just before sleep. So what does a full day of Nitnem actually take? And is everyone doing exactly the same thing? Two plain questions, with two plain answers, and neither of them is meant to scare anyone off.
screen: `READ THE RECIPE FIRST.` → `SEVEN BANIS SO FAR.` → `WHAT DOES IT REALLY TAKE?`

segments.voice: First, the time. The morning banis are the long part: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai and all of Anand, read at a steady pace, fill most of the hour. Someone who has said them every day for years goes faster. Rehras in the evening is shorter. Kirtan Sohila at night takes only a few minutes. So a full Nitnem is an hour or more across the day. Second, the differences. Sikhs share the core, but not every detail is the same everywhere. The Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht lists three morning banis; other Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five. Some traditions, like the Damdami Taksal and some jathas, recite a longer Rehras or a longer Chaupai. Some Sikhs add more banis on top, like Sukhmani or Asa di Var in the morning. These are differences of practice within one faith, not a ranking of who prays properly. Third, the most useful thing. Sikhs who have taken amrit commit to Nitnem as part of their vows. For many others, and certainly for learners, it's normal to grow into it. A child might learn the Mul Mantar first, then Japji's first pauri, then more. An adult coming back to the faith might begin with Japji alone, or Sohila at night. Nobody arrives at the full hour on day one. Nitnem means the daily rule, and its weight is on daily. One bani, said every day, becomes a path worn across a field.
screen: `AN HOUR OR MORE A DAY.` · `THE CORE, AND THE DIFFERENCES.` · `A VOW FOR SOME, A ROAD FOR OTHERS.` · `STEADINESS OVER SIZE.` · then, large: `START WITH ONE.`

segments.voice: Pick one bani to begin with. Close your eyes, and don't run through a list. Wait a moment and see which one comes back on its own: a line, a tune, a picture. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that comes back. Hold it in mind now, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
How long it takes. A full Nitnem is an hour or more a day, with small differences between traditions, and many grow into it one bani at a time.
Your line: start with one. Today, find the bani you picked, in a gutka, an app or a recording, and save it where you'll see it tomorrow. Day one hundred thirty-six.

notes: Durations are rough estimates (Japji 15–20 min, morning ~1 hour, Rehras 15–20, Sohila ~5); they vary with pace. Confirm.
Differences named: Damdami Taksal and some jathas reciting a longer Rehras/Chaupai; additions such as Sukhmani or Asa di Var. Confirm the framing is fair and neutral.
Framing that Amritdhari Sikhs commit to Nitnem while learners 'grow into it' is meant not to make Nitnem sound optional for those under vows. Confirm.
Trapdoor link between the five morning banis and the Amrit ceremony's five banis: confirm.
